subject: Biology
title: Mendel and His Peas
description: A short lesson to help you apply Mendel and His Peas.

hook.text: In the 1860s, a monk named Gregor Mendel grew thousands of pea plants in a monastery garden.

buildup.text: He tracked traits like color and height across generations, recording every result.

discovery.text: Mendel found that traits come in pairs and one form can dominate the other.

twist.text: His work was ignored for 35 years. He died without knowing he founded modern genetics.

climax.text: In 1900, three scientists independently rediscovered Mendel's laws and changed biology forever.

punchline.text: A monk and his peas invented genetics.

quiz.question: What organism did Mendel use in his famous genetics experiments?

details.summary: Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, discovered the fundamental laws of inheritance by studying pea plants in the 1860s. His experiments with traits like seed color and plant height revealed dominant and recessive alleles and the mathematical ratios of inheritance.
details.whyItMatters: Mendel's work founded the science of genetics. His laws of segregation and independent assortment remain the foundation for understanding heredity, from breeding programs to medical genetics and evolutionary biology.
takeaways: Mendel tracked seven discrete traits across thousands of pea plants
The 3:1 ratio in F2 generations revealed dominant and recessive inheritance
Mendel's work was rediscovered in 1900, decades after his 1866 publication

faq.question: Why did Mendel choose pea plants for his experiments?
faq.answer: Peas have easily observable discrete traits, reproduce quickly, and can be either self-pollinated or cross-pollinated under controlled conditions. This allowed Mendel to track inheritance patterns precisely across multiple generations with large sample sizes.

faq.question: Why was Mendel's work ignored for 35 years?
faq.answer: Mendel published in a minor journal and his mathematical approach was unfamiliar to biologists. The scientific community lacked the concepts to appreciate his findings. When three scientists independently rediscovered his principles in 1900, his genius was finally recognized.
